current_state_summary: The region is in the middle of an interstate war. On 28 Feb 2026 at 01:15 the US and Israel launched Operation Epic Fury / Operation Roaring Lion against Iran; Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed in the opening hours. Mojtaba Khamenei was installed as Supreme Leader on 8 Mar 2026 and has made no public appearance since. The IRGC declared the Strait of Hormuz closed on 2-4 Mar 2026 — the first sustained >50% Hormuz disruption in history. Gulf producers shut in 7.5 mb/d of crude in March and 9.1 mb/d in April; the IEA called it the largest supply disruption in oil-market history. Brent peaked at $116.29 on 9 Mar (physical cargoes reported $130-150), a ~51-65% monthly rise, the largest on record. A Pakistan-brokered ceasefire took effect 8 Apr; Iran re-restricted passage 19 Apr. Trump and Pezeshkian remotely signed a 14-point MOU (the Islamabad Memorandum) on 17 Jun 2026 with a 60-day ceasefire extension; the US issued sweeping oil sanctions waivers on 23 Jun. The MOU collapsed in July over an unresolved dispute about which Hormuz lanes vessels must use: Iran struck at least nine commercial ships from 6 Jul, the US revoked the oil waiver on 7 Jul, Trump declared the deal 'over', and 13 consecutive nights of US bombing followed alongside a US blockade disabling roughly one Iranian-linked ship per day. On 12-13 Jul Iran fired missiles and drones at five Gulf states (Al Udeid in Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, UAE, Oman) and Jordan; on 18 Jul Iranian ballistic missiles hit Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, killing two US service members. Hormuz transits fell to 53 vessels in the week to 20 Jul, -66% w/w; tanker and gas-carrier crossings fell from 90 to 30. Houthis resumed Red Sea attacks (MT Encelia, MT Layla) and declared a blockade on Saudi-linked shipping, effectively closing Bab el-Mandeb; Saudi Arabia rerouted Asian crude via Suez. Brent topped $100 on 23 Jul, then fell ~16% in three sessions to $87.53 on 28 Jul as the US paused strikes; Iran says no talks are under way. War-risk insurance for Hormuz transits runs 3-10% of hull value (norm ~5%) versus 0.25% pre-war. Cumulative deaths across all fronts are roughly 9,000-18,000: Iran 3,468 (official) to 6,000+ (US/Israeli estimates), Lebanon 4,328 since 2 Mar, Israel 57, US 13-15. On Iran's nuclear file, the IAEA has had no access to any of the four declared enrichment facilities for over a year; the last verified 60% U-235 stockpile is 440.9 kg UF6 plus 184.1 kg at 20%; Iran's FM said on 15 Mar 2026 the HEU is 'under the rubble' with no plan to recover it; Israeli intelligence believes thousands of centrifuges were moved to Pickaxe Mountain. The March 2026 US worldwide threat assessment does not assess that Iran has decided to weaponise. Elsewhere: the Gaza ceasefire of Oct 2025 holds at phase 1 with phase 2 stalled — Israel's cabinet approved ISF entry on 26 Jul (initial ~200 troops). Israel-Hezbollah ceasefires from 16 Apr and 1 Jun are fragile. Syria's al-Sharaa is negotiating a security agreement with Israel. Saudi Arabia signed a 30-year US civil nuclear deal in July that Trump says bars enrichment and is conditioned on normalisation with Israel; Riyadh publicly re-anchored normalisation to an irreversible path to Palestinian statehood. The Knesset dissolved on 17 Jul; Israeli elections are set for 27 Oct 2026 with the opposition bloc leading 69-51. Iran's rial passed 1.47m/USD, CPI inflation exceeds 42%, and nationwide protests across all 31 provinces from 28 Dec 2025 were suppressed by mass arrests and internet blackouts.

indicators.label: Middle East composite conflict intensity index (0-100)
indicators.source: Composite constructed from ACLED Middle East event/fatality counts, UCDP state-based conflict data, CFR Global Conflict Tracker, and CENTCOM/IDF operational reporting. Anchors: 2011-2019 average ~30, post-Oct-2023 Gaza war ~55, Jun 2025 12-day war ~70, Mar 2026 Epic Fury peak ~95.

indicators.label: Iran stockpile of UF6 enriched to 60% U-235 (last IAEA-verified / best estimate)
indicators.source: IAEA GOV/2026 Iran verification reports as analysed by ISIS (isis-online.org) and the Arms Control Association 'Status of Iran's Nuclear Program' factsheet. Note: IAEA has had no access to declared enrichment facilities since mid-2025 and cannot verify size, composition or location; Iran claims the material is entombed at Esfahan/Natanz.

indicators.label: Global nuclear proliferation pressure index (0-100)
indicators.source: Composite from Arms Control Association, Carnegie, Just Security 'In 2026, a Growing Risk of Nuclear Proliferation', SIPRI Yearbook. Components: number of states with active weapons debates, NPT stress events, extended-deterrence credibility, testing moratorium status. Anchors: 2000s ~30, 2015 (JCPOA) ~25, 2020 ~35, 2023 ~45, 2025 ~60.

indicators.label: Suez Canal transits below 2023 baseline
indicators.source: Lloyd's List Intelligence / Suez Canal Authority via Splash247 and gCaptain ('Suez traffic still 60% down 100 days after last Houthi attack', Jan 2026); Houthi blockade of Saudi-linked shipping declared July 2026 partly offset by Saudi crude rerouting north through Suez.

indicators.label: Geopolitical risk premium embedded in Brent (Brent minus fundamentals-implied price)
indicators.source: Derived: Brent $87.53 (TradingEconomics, 28 Jul 2026) less an estimated ~$61 fundamentals-implied level from EIA STEO pre-conflict 2026 balances and OPEC+ spare capacity. Cross-checked against the March 2026 peak of $116.29 (premium ~$55) and pre-conflict 2025 average premium of ~$3-5.

indicators.label: Total oil (crude, condensate, products) flowing through the Strait of Hormuz
indicators.source: EIA World Oil Transit Chokepoints (baseline 20-21 mb/d in 2023-24); current level from Lloyd's List Intelligence transit counts via USNI News and CNBC ('more than 8 million barrels transited Hormuz Sunday with military assistance', 13 Jul 2026).

indicators.label: Brent crude front-month price
indicators.source: TradingEconomics / ICE Brent front-month; corroborated by Fortune daily oil price page for 28 Jul 2026 ($89.08 intraday) and CNN reporting Brent above $100 on 23 Jul before a ~16% three-session decline.

indicators.label: Islamic Republic regime stability index (100 = fully consolidated)
indicators.source: Composite from BTI 2026 Iran country report, Wikipedia 'Iran internal crisis (2025-present)', UK House of Commons Library CBP-10456, Iran International. Inputs: nationwide protests across all 31 provinces from 28 Dec 2025, CPI inflation >42%, rial >1.47m/USD, decapitation of the Supreme Leader, successful but costly security crackdown. Anchors: 2015 ~70, 2019 ~60, 2022 Mahsa protests ~50, 2024 ~52, Jan 2026 ~35.

indicators.label: Share of required IAEA verification activities being conducted in Iran
indicators.source: IAEA Iran verification and monitoring reports (GOV/2026 series) as analysed by ISIS, June 2026: no access to any of the four declared enrichment facilities, unknown status of the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant, no continuity of knowledge on the enriched-uranium stockpile. Residual access is essentially Bushehr-related safeguards only.

indicators.label: Marine war-risk premium for a Strait of Hormuz transit, as share of hull value
indicators.source: Lloyd's List, AGBI ('Gulf shipping cover still available as premiums hit 10%', Jul 2026), The National (17 Jul 2026: 3-10% of hull value, up from 0.25% pre-war), S&P Global Commodity Insights.

indicators.label: Iranian crude and condensate exports
indicators.source: Kpler and Vortexa tanker tracking via CNBC and Iran International; pre-war baseline 1.39 mb/d (Jan 2026, Kpler) with ~90% going to China. Current level depressed by the US interdiction campaign ('a ship a day') and revocation of the 23 Jun sanctions waiver on 7 Jul 2026.

indicators.label: Suez Canal annualised transit revenue (Egypt)
indicators.source: Suez Canal Authority via Washington Post and Middle East Institute reporting; 2023 peak $10.25bn, 2024 ~$4.0bn, end-2025 ~$4bn. Current annualised run-rate is a mid-2026 estimate incorporating partial container-line returns (CMA CGM, Maersk) offset by renewed Houthi attacks.

indicators.label: Gaza ceasefire integrity index (100 = fully implemented 20-point plan)
indicators.source: Composite from FDD Long War Journal ceasefire-violation tracking (13 IDF-claimed violations 30 Jun-9 Jul 2026), UN Security Council Report July 2026 monthly forecast, J Street 'Nine Months In'. Phase 1 complete (hostages released, ceasefire holding); phase 2 (Hamas disarmament, ISF deployment, governance) stalled but ISF entry approved by the Israeli cabinet on 26 Jul 2026.

indicators.label: Israel-Hezbollah conflict intensity index (0-100)
indicators.source: Composite from ACLED Lebanon event data, Lebanese Ministry of Public Health casualty reporting (4,328 killed since 2 Mar 2026), and Wikipedia '2026 Lebanon war' / '2026 Israel-Lebanon ceasefire'. Anchors: 2007-2022 baseline ~8, Oct 2023-Nov 2024 ~60, Mar-Apr 2026 war ~90, post-1 Jun 2026 ceasefire with continuing Israeli strikes ~34.

indicators.label: Saudi-Israel normalisation progress index (100 = full diplomatic relations)
indicators.source: Composite from MEI ('Normalization is slipping away'), INSS, Axios/Washington Times reporting on the July 2026 US-Saudi 30-year civil nuclear agreement conditioned on Abraham Accords accession, and Saudi statements (May 2026) rejecting normalisation absent an irreversible path to Palestinian statehood. Anchors: Sep 2023 pre-Oct-7 peak ~55, mid-2025 ~42, post-Feb-2026 war ~20.

indicators.label: Days in the trailing 90 with direct state-on-state strikes between Iran and Israel/US
indicators.source: Constructed from CENTCOM operational releases, Al Jazeera and CNN live-blog day counts (13 consecutive nights of US bombing in July 2026; four Iranian missile attacks on US bases in Jordan in one week), Operation Epic Fury DoD fact sheets.

events.statement: A new major direct military campaign against Iran by Israel and/or the United States: at least 7 consecutive days of strikes on Iranian territory, beginning on or after 1 October 2026.
events.resolution_criteria: CENTCOM, IDF or Iranian government confirmation, corroborated by at least two of Reuters/AP/AFP, that strikes on targets inside Iran occurred on 7 or more consecutive days with a start date on or after 1 Oct 2026. Isolated retaliatory salvos, covert sabotage and strikes confined to Iranian proxies outside Iran do not count.
events.reference_class: Recurrence of interstate hostilities after a ceasefire that leaves the core dispute unsettled: Correlates of War / Fortna data show roughly one third of such ceasefires break down into renewed major fighting within five years (~8%/yr), rising to ~35-45%/yr where the casus belli is an ongoing weapons programme. Direct Israel/US-Iran state-on-state campaigns: zero in 1979-2023, then five rounds in 27 months (Apr 2024, Oct 2024, Jun 2025, Feb-Apr 2026, Jul 2026) ~= 2.2/yr in the acute period. Blended reference rate ~0.30/yr.
events.reasoning: Base rate 0.30/yr from blended ceasefire-recurrence and observed 2024-26 frequency. Multiplier 1.9 because the June 2026 MOU has already collapsed once over an unresolved Hormuz transit-lane dispute, Iran states no talks are under way, no final nuclear agreement exists, Iran is reconstituting missile production, and Israel's 27 Oct election creates an incentive for demonstrated toughness — partially offset by mutual exhaustion, Trump's stated preference for a deal, and Iran's degraded capacity. 0.30 x 1.9 = 0.57/yr. Cumulative from 1 Oct 2026: 1-(1-0.57)^1.25 = 0.50 for end-2027, nudged to 0.55 because the current pause is explicitly tactical rather than a ceasefire. Raw compounding gives 0.97 by 2030 and 0.999 by 2036, which over-predicts: the hazard must decay as either a settlement, a regime change, or a stable armistice emerges, so I apply a declining hazard path yielding 0.81 and 0.89. This is the highest-probability event in the set and it should be, because the region is currently at war.

events.statement: Total oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz fall at least 50% below the 2023-24 baseline of roughly 20 mb/d for at least 30 consecutive days, at any point on or after 1 September 2026.
events.resolution_criteria: EIA, IEA, Kpler or Vortexa published flow data showing Hormuz total oil throughput at or below 10 mb/d on a 30-day rolling average, with the window starting on or after 1 Sep 2026.
events.reference_class: Sustained (>=30-day, >=50%) Hormuz oil-flow disruptions, 1980-2025: zero. The Tanker War (1984-88) produced 450+ ship attacks without ever cutting flows by half for a month; the 1987-88 US escort operations, the 2019 limpet-mine attacks and the June 2025 12-day war all failed to do so. The first-ever such episode occurred in Mar-Apr 2026 (7.5-9.1 mb/d of Gulf production shut in; IEA: largest supply disruption in oil-market history), with a near-miss in Jul 2026. Historical frequency 1/46 years ~= 0.022/yr.
events.reasoning: This is one of the rare cases where a multiplier above 3 is defensible and I justify it explicitly: the event moved from never-observed to twice-in-six-months. Iran demonstrated in March 2026 that it can and will do this, the taboo and the uncertainty about Iranian resolve are both gone, the specific dispute that triggered July's attacks (which lanes vessels must use) is unresolved, and Hormuz is now Iran's principal remaining escalation lever after the destruction of its navy and much of its missile force. Observed 2026 frequency is ~2/yr; an 8x multiplier on the 0.03 historical base gives only 0.24/yr, which is conservative for the next twelve months and appropriate as a multi-year blend. Near-term hazard ~0.45/yr gives p_by_2027 = 0.42; decaying to ~0.15/yr through 2030 gives 0.42 + 0.58*0.386 = 0.63; decaying to ~0.06/yr thereafter gives 0.74. The decay reflects that a durable settlement, US escorting/convoying at scale, or Iranian capability attrition each plausibly retire the risk.

events.statement: Renewed major Israel-Hezbollah hostilities: at least 14 consecutive days of Israeli strikes in Lebanon together with at least 200 Hezbollah rockets, missiles or drones fired at Israel, beginning on or after 1 September 2026.
events.resolution_criteria: IDF and Lebanese Ministry of Public Health / UNIFIL reporting, corroborated by two major wires, meeting both thresholds within a single continuous episode starting on or after 1 Sep 2026.
events.reference_class: Major Israel-Hezbollah rounds since Hezbollah's formation: 1993 (Accountability), 1996 (Grapes of Wrath), 2006 (Second Lebanon War), Oct 2023-Nov 2024, Mar-Apr 2026 = 5 in 33 years = 0.15/yr. Ceasefire durability: the Nov 2024 ceasefire collapsed into full war within 15 months; the 2006 ceasefire held 17 years.
events.reasoning: Base rate 0.15/yr. Multiplier 2.2: the current arrangement is a stack of short extensions (16 Apr 10-day truce, 23 Apr three weeks, 15 May 45 days, 1 Jun Israel-Hezbollah understanding) rather than a settlement; Qassem stated on 27 Apr that Hezbollah will not revert to the pre-March status and will respond to Israeli attacks; Hezbollah initially rejected the 3 Jun Israel-Lebanon deal; disarmament is unresolved and Israeli strikes continue. Offsetting: Hezbollah lost 4,328 dead and much of its leadership and arsenal, Iran's resupply corridor through Syria is gone under al-Sharaa, and the Lebanese state is actively pushing disarmament — which is why the multiplier is 2.2 and not higher. 0.15 x 2.2 = 0.33/yr. 1-(1-0.33)^1.35 = 0.38; I use 0.34 because the very degraded Hezbollah needs reconstitution time. Compounding with modest hazard decay gives 0.63 by 2030 and 0.79 by 2036.

events.statement: Major collapse of the October 2025 Gaza ceasefire: resumption of Israeli ground or air operations causing at least 500 Palestinian deaths in any 30-day window, or a formal Israeli or US declaration terminating the ceasefire.
events.resolution_criteria: Gaza Ministry of Health figures (or OCHA/UN casualty reporting) showing >=500 conflict deaths in a 30-day window after 1 Sep 2026, or an official Israeli cabinet or US Board of Peace statement declaring the ceasefire ended.
events.reference_class: Israel-Hamas ceasefires 2008-2026: Jun 2008 (collapsed after ~5 months), Nov 2012 (held ~1.5 yrs), Aug 2014 (held with flare-ups ~7 yrs), May 2021 (held), Nov 2023 (collapsed after 7 days), Jan 2025 (collapsed after ~8 weeks), Oct 2025 (holding 9+ months). Three of seven collapsed within a year, giving ~0.35/yr for a fresh ceasefire; conditional on surviving nine months the hazard falls to roughly 0.20-0.25/yr.
events.reasoning: Base rate 0.25/yr conditional on nine months of survival. Multiplier only 1.1 because the pressures roughly balance: phase 2 is stalled with Hamas undisarmed and the IDF claiming 13 violations in the ten days to 9 Jul, but the ISF is finally entering with Israeli cabinet approval (26 Jul), the Board of Peace pilot zone at Tel Sultan is proceeding, Trump remains personally invested, and an incumbent Israeli government facing a 27 Oct election in which it trails 51-69 has little appetite for reopening Gaza. Both parties are assessed as preferring the status quo. 0.25 x 1.1 = 0.275/yr. 1-(1-0.275)^1.35 = 0.34, set to 0.32; with hazard decaying as the ISF consolidates, 0.60 by 2030 and 0.77 by 2036.

events.statement: A GCC state (Saudi Arabia, UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain, Oman) undergoes an irregular change of head of state or government, a sustained armed insurgency, or nationwide unrest producing at least 100 protest-related deaths or requiring foreign military intervention.
events.resolution_criteria: Coup, forced abdication or extra-constitutional leadership change reported by two major wires; or ACLED/Amnesty-documented >=100 protest-related deaths within 12 months in a single GCC state; or deployment of Peninsula Shield or other foreign forces into a GCC state for internal security. Routine hereditary succession does not count.
events.reference_class: GCC states 1971-2026 = 330 state-years. Qualifying events: Saudi 1979 Grand Mosque seizure (~250 deaths), Qatar 1995 palace coup, Bahrain 2011 uprising with Peninsula Shield intervention. Oman's 1970 coup and Dhofar insurgency sit at the window edge. Roughly 3-4 events / 330 state-years = 0.011 per state-year, or 0.055-0.070 per year for the region as a whole.
events.reasoning: Base rate 0.055/yr region-wide. Multiplier 1.9: Gulf states have now been physically struck repeatedly (Riyadh and eastern Saudi Arabia, three killed in the UAE, Al Udeid, Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman), the US security guarantee has been publicly stress-tested, Houthis have declared a blockade on Saudi shipping, and Saudi succession risk is non-trivial with King Salman around 90. Strongly offsetting: rally-round-the-flag effects, extremely high coercive capacity, and — importantly — a high oil price is fiscally stabilising for every GCC government, which is why I give oil price a negative elasticity here. Gulf monarchies have survived the Iran-Iraq war, 1990-91, 2011 and 2019 without regime change. 0.055 x 1.9 = 0.105/yr. 1-(1-0.105)^1.4 = 0.14, trimmed to 0.11 since the near-term shock has already been absorbed without incident; 0.28 by 2030 and 0.44 by 2036 with mild hazard decay. Note this covers six states, so the per-state decade probability is only ~9%.

events.statement: The Israel/US-Iran conflict expands to sustained direct combat participation by at least two additional states as belligerents (at least 30 days of offensive military operations each), drawn from Saudi Arabia, UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain, Oman, Turkey, Egypt, Jordan, Pakistan, Iraq as a state, or Russia.
events.resolution_criteria: Official acknowledgement by the governments concerned, or corroborated reporting by two of Reuters/AP/AFP plus IISS or CSIS assessment, that two or more listed states conducted offensive military operations against a belligerent for >=30 days. Air and missile defence interception, basing, overflight and logistics do not count.
events.reference_class: Regional wars that pulled in >=2 additional state belligerents: 1948, 1967 and 1973 Arab-Israeli wars, 1990-91 Gulf War, and the Syrian civil war over a decade — roughly 5 of 12 major post-1945 Middle East wars, but expansion typically occurs within the first year or not at all. Counter-cases are strong: the 1980-88 Iran-Iraq war drew in no additional state belligerents in eight years despite the Tanker War, and in 2023-2026, 33 months of Gaza, Lebanon and Iran wars have produced no new state belligerent even after Gulf capitals were struck. Conditional hazard ~0.05/yr given an ongoing regional war.
events.reasoning: Base rate 0.05/yr conditional on an ongoing regional war. Multiplier 2.0: Iran has now struck six Arab states plus Jordan, US personnel were killed on Jordanian soil, the Houthis have declared a blockade on Saudi shipping driving Bab el-Mandeb exports to near zero, and the Saudi-Pakistan Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement of 17 Sep 2025 creates a formal tripwire. But the revealed preference is overwhelmingly for non-belligerency: after Iranian salvos hit Gulf skylines in March, the GCC states issued a joint condemnation of both sides rather than entering; Turkey is actively mediating and explicitly wants to avoid spillover; Egypt is financially incapable; Jordan intercepts but does not strike. 0.05 x 2.0 = 0.10/yr. 1-(1-0.10)^1.35 = 0.13, trimmed to 0.11 since the highest-risk moment (July's Gulf strikes) has already passed without entry; 0.26 by 2030 and 0.37 by 2036.

events.statement: Iran formally withdraws from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty under Article X.
events.resolution_criteria: Iran deposits or transmits formal notice of withdrawal to the NPT depositaries and the UN Security Council, confirmed by the IAEA Secretariat or the UN, regardless of whether the three-month notice period has elapsed.
events.reference_class: Article X withdrawals 1970-2026: one (North Korea, announced 1993, effected 2003) among ~190 states parties over 56 years. Conditional class — NPT parties whose nuclear facilities were militarily attacked: Iraq 1981 and 1991 (did not withdraw), Syria 2007 (did not withdraw), Iran 2025 and 2026 (has not withdrawn in 13 months of threats). Conditional rate ~0.02/yr.
events.reasoning: Base rate 0.02/yr from the attacked-NPT-party conditional class. Multiplier 4.5 exceeds 3 and I justify it: Iran is already in de facto withdrawal — the IAEA has had no access to any declared enrichment facility for over a year, the Majlis has an active withdrawal bill (introduced 17 Jun 2025, revived March 2026), UN snapback sanctions returned on 27 Sep 2025 removing much of the residual benefit of membership, and Iranian officials openly describe withdrawal as leverage. The restraint is that withdrawal forfeits Iran's strongest remaining diplomatic card and would likely trigger further strikes, which is exactly why it has been threatened repeatedly and never executed. 0.02 x 4.5 = 0.09/yr. 1-(1-0.09)^1.4 = 0.12, set to 0.13; with hazard decaying if a comprehensive deal lands, 0.29 by 2030 and 0.42 by 2036.

events.statement: Iran produces at least 25 kg of weapons-grade (>=90% U-235) uranium, one significant quantity, or an equivalent quantity of separated weapons-grade plutonium.
events.resolution_criteria: An IAEA report, a public assessment issued or confirmed by at least two of the US, UK, France or Israel governments, or an Iranian official declaration, stating that Iran has produced >=1 significant quantity of weapons-grade fissile material.
events.reference_class: Nuclear-threshold states that crossed to weapons-grade production: of roughly 10 states that reached a credible threshold capability since 1960 (Israel, South Africa, Pakistan, India, North Korea, Taiwan, South Korea, Brazil, Argentina, Iran), about 5 crossed and 5 did not, over an average threshold tenure of ~10-15 years — roughly 3-4% per threshold-state-year. Iran specifically has held near-breakout capability since 2021 and has not crossed in five years.
events.reasoning: Base rate 0.035/yr per threshold-state-year. Multiplier 2.2 nets two large opposing forces. Motive is sharply up: Iran has been attacked twice in twelve months, its Supreme Leader was assassinated, restraint demonstrably failed to protect it, and the deterrence argument now dominates Tehran's internal debate. Means are sharply down: Natanz was destroyed and Fordow and Isfahan badly damaged in June 2025 and again in Feb-Apr 2026, the 440.9 kg of 60% HEU is assessed by Iran's own foreign minister to be 'under the rubble', and independent assessments put the realistic weapon timeline at 2.5 years or more absent foreign assistance. Detection remains highly likely and would trigger immediate further strikes. 0.035 x 2.2 = 0.077/yr in steady state, but the near term is capability-constrained, so p_by_2027 is only 0.05 rather than the 0.10 that naive compounding gives. Unconstrained compounding gives 0.30 by 2030 and 0.56 by 2036; I discount to 0.24 and 0.40 for the destroyed infrastructure, the possibility of a comprehensive deal, and the observed five-year record of Iranian restraint at the threshold.

events.statement: Iran conducts a nuclear explosive test.
events.resolution_criteria: CTBTO International Monitoring System seismic detection consistent with a nuclear explosion at an Iranian site, plus either radionuclide confirmation, US Geological Survey/AFTAC attribution, or an Iranian government claim confirmed by at least two of the US, UK or France.
events.reference_class: First nuclear tests by new possessor states, 1945-2026: US 1945, USSR 1949, UK 1952, France 1960, China 1964, India 1974, Pakistan 1998, North Korea 2006 = 8 in 81 years, i.e. ~0.10/yr globally across all aspirants. Of the states that acquired weapons, 3 of 5 post-1970 possessors tested overtly (India, Pakistan, DPRK) while Israel and South Africa did not, giving P(overt test | possession) ~= 0.45-0.6. No state has tested since 2017 and the world passed eight years without a test in January 2026.
events.reasoning: This event is essentially conditional on iran_nuclear_breakout, so it must be internally consistent with it. Base rate 0.008/yr for a specific threshold state testing. Multiplier 2.5 because the global testing moratorium is eroding (New START expired in Feb 2026, the US accused China of supercritical testing and announced its own intent to resume testing) and because Iran's experience of being decapitated while ambiguous raises the demonstration value of an overt test relative to a normal proliferator. Consistency check: P(breakout by 2036) = 0.40 x P(overt test | material, within window) ~= 0.45 gives 0.18, which is what I use for p_by_2036. Testing typically lags first fissile material by 1-3 years, so p_by_2030 = 0.24 x 0.45 x 0.65 = 0.07 and p_by_2027 is near zero at 0.008. Confidence is low because the conditional test probability for a state that would face immediate military retaliation is genuinely unknown.

events.statement: A state other than the current nine possessors (US, Russia, UK, France, China, India, Pakistan, North Korea, Israel) is confirmed to possess an assembled nuclear weapon or at least one significant quantity of weapons-grade fissile material under military control.
events.resolution_criteria: IAEA confirmation, or a public assessment issued or endorsed by at least two of the US, UK and France governments, or an official declaration by the state itself, that the state possesses an assembled nuclear weapon or >=1 SQ of weapons-grade fissile material under military control.
events.reference_class: New nuclear weapon states 1945-2026: nine acquired over 81 years = 0.111/yr, but the rate has collapsed — the last new possessor was North Korea around 2006, giving zero in the past 20 years, and four states (South Africa, Ukraine, Belarus, Kazakhstan) gave weapons up. Rate over 1990-2026 (36 years): 1 = 0.028/yr.
events.reasoning: Base rate 0.028/yr. Multiplier 2.6 rather than something larger: the drivers are real — New START expired in Feb 2026 with no successor, US extended-deterrence credibility is openly questioned in Seoul, Tokyo and Riyadh, MBS has repeatedly said Saudi Arabia will match any Iranian weapon, the Saudi-Pakistan defence pact of Sep 2025 institutionalises outsourced deterrence, and Washington is actively supporting South Korean fissile-material-adjacent capabilities — but decision-to-weapon lead times are 5-15 years, detection risk is high, and the US July 2026 Saudi civil nuclear agreement explicitly bars enrichment. Probabilities must dominate iran_nuclear_breakout since Iran is a member of this event class: 0.055 > 0.05 by 2027, 0.28 > 0.24 by 2030, 0.46 > 0.40 by 2036. The increment over Iran alone (roughly 4-6 percentage points by 2036) reflects Saudi Arabia, South Korea and, further out, Turkey and Japan.

events.statement: The Islamic Republic ceases to govern Iran: the office of Supreme Leader is abolished or vacated without a clerical successor, or a government not derived from the Islamic Republic's constitutional order controls Tehran for at least 30 consecutive days.
events.resolution_criteria: Recognition by at least three UN Security Council permanent members, or reporting by two of Reuters/AP/AFP plus a UN or IAEA operational statement, that a non-Islamic-Republic authority exercises effective control of Tehran for >=30 days, or formal abolition of the velayat-e faqih.
events.reference_class: Failure of consolidated personalist/theocratic authoritarian regimes: Geddes, Wright and Frantz data give ~4-5%/yr for personalist regimes overall, falling to ~2-3%/yr for regimes older than 30 years with a coup-proofed parallel military. The Islamic Republic has survived 1980-88 total war, 1999, 2009, 2017-18, 2019 and 2022 mass uprisings, and now decapitation.
events.reasoning: Base rate 0.03/yr. Multiplier 2.8: protests spread to all 31 provinces from 28 Dec 2025, the rial passed 1.47m/USD with CPI inflation above 42% and food inflation near 75%, the Supreme Leader was assassinated, his successor has not been seen in public in nearly five months and issues statements only in writing, oil exports have been interdicted to a fraction of pre-war levels, and Iran has lost its navy, much of its missile force and its regional proxy architecture. Restraining factors keep this well below journalistic estimates: the January crackdown worked (mass arrests, internet blackouts, de facto curfews), the IRGC remains cohesive and has consolidated rather than fractured, there is no organised opposition holding territory, no significant elite defection, and external war historically produces rally effects. 0.03 x 2.8 = 0.084/yr. 1-(1-0.084)^1.4 = 0.11, set to 0.10; 0.27 by 2030 and 0.42 by 2036 with hazard decaying if the war ends. Confidence low: authoritarian collapse is the least predictable event class in political science.

events.statement: The United States and Iran conclude a comprehensive nuclear agreement beyond the June 2026 MOU, and IAEA inspectors are physically readmitted to Natanz, Fordow and Isfahan for at least 90 consecutive days.
events.resolution_criteria: A signed US-Iran agreement (or a UNSC-endorsed equivalent) covering enrichment limits and HEU disposition, together with IAEA Director General confirmation that Agency inspectors have had continuous access to all three named sites for >=90 days.
events.reference_class: Major negotiated nuclear settlements following proliferation crises: Agreed Framework 1994, Libya 2003, the Six-Party Joint Statement 2005 (collapsed), JCPOA 2015 — roughly 4 concluded agreements across ~5 sustained crisis tracks over 45 years, giving ~0.08 per crisis-year. Note that half of these subsequently collapsed, and the June 2026 MOU has already collapsed once within a month.
events.reasoning: Base rate 0.08 per crisis-year. Multiplier 1.5: a 14-point framework text already exists and was signed by both heads of state on 17 Jun 2026, Trump is personally invested and repeatedly signals he wants a deal, Qatar, Pakistan and Oman are actively mediating, and the economic pain on both sides is extreme (Iranian exports near zero, oil above $100 hurting the US administration domestically). Offsetting and keeping the multiplier modest: the MOU collapsed within a month over an unresolved Hormuz lane dispute, Iran publicly says no talks are under way, the new Iranian leadership is drawn from the IRGC, and the 27 Oct Israeli election freezes Israeli flexibility until at least early 2027. 0.08 x 1.5 = 0.12/yr. 1-(1-0.12)^1.4 = 0.16; 0.39 by 2030 and 0.58 by 2036. This event is deliberately included as the principal de-escalatory branch — most Monte Carlo runs should not end in escalation.

events.statement: Saudi Arabia and Israel establish full diplomatic relations.
events.resolution_criteria: A signed normalisation agreement or joint announcement of the establishment of full diplomatic relations, followed by the announced opening of embassies or the exchange of ambassadors, confirmed by both governments.
events.reference_class: Arab state normalisations with Israel: Egypt 1979, Jordan 1994, UAE, Bahrain, Morocco and Sudan 2020 = 6 events in 47 years across ~20 Arab states. For a specific major Arab state under active US-brokered negotiation, roughly 0.05/yr; Saudi Arabia has been 'close' repeatedly since 2020 and has never concluded.
events.reasoning: This is one of the few cases where current conditions LOWER the hazard, and the multiplier is deliberately below 1.0. In May 2026 Riyadh publicly rejected joining the Abraham Accords and re-anchored normalisation to a clear and irreversible path to Palestinian statehood; a Saudi royal source stated normalisation will not happen under the current Netanyahu government; Gaza phase 2 is stalled; and Israel's Knesset dissolved on 17 Jul with an election on 27 Oct, freezing any Israeli concession until at least Q1 2027. The offsetting force is real and growing: Trump tied the 30-year US-Saudi civil nuclear agreement signed in July 2026 explicitly to Abraham Accords accession, giving Riyadh a concrete prize. 0.05 x 0.7 = 0.035/yr near term, giving p_by_2027 = 0.05. The hazard should rise materially after October if the opposition bloc (currently leading 69-51 in Kan 11 polling, with Eisenkot's Yashar level with Likud) forms a government willing to use two-state language, so I use a rising path: 0.26 by 2030 and 0.48 by 2036.

couplings.mechanism: War risk is repriced into Gulf barrels essentially contemporaneously. Brent rose ~51% in March 2026 within three weeks of the IRGC's Hormuz closure declaration, and fell ~16% in three sessions in late July on a US strike pause.

Charterers and owners withdraw tonnage within days of kinetic escalation. Lloyd's List recorded a 51.9% fall in Hormuz transits in the week after 9 July 2026 and a further drop to 53 vessels (-66%) in the week to 20 July.

Roughly 20 mb/d of oil, about a fifth of global consumption, moves through Hormuz, and most OPEC+ spare capacity sits behind it. Gulf producers shut in 7.5 mb/d in March and 9.1 mb/d in April 2026; cumulative supply loss exceeded 360 Mb in March alone.

Definitional: the risk premium is the wedge between the observed Brent price and the fundamentals-implied level, so it passes through near one-for-one, damped slightly by simultaneous demand destruction at high prices.

Lloyd's war-risk syndicates reprice Joint War Committee listed areas within days of attacks. Hormuz hull premiums went from 0.25% of hull value pre-war to 3-10% (norm ~5%) by July 2026, i.e. $3-10m on a $100m tanker.

Above roughly 5% of hull value, the insurance cost exceeds the voyage margin for most crude and product trades, and some underwriters withdraw cover entirely, so tonnage exits with a one-quarter charter-cycle lag.

Houthi operational tempo tracks the Iran-Israel-US conflict cycle with a short lag; attacks resumed in July 2026 within two weeks of the MOU collapse, after roughly eight months of quiescence during which carriers had begun returning to Suez.

Near-mechanical: Suez transit fees are volume-linked. Egyptian canal revenue fell from $10.25bn in 2023 to about $4bn in 2024-25 as transits fell ~60%, with roughly a quarter's lag from booking to receipt.

Iran suspends safeguards cooperation as a retaliatory and protective measure after strikes on nuclear sites, as it did after June 2025 and again after February 2026; access recovery requires a negotiated framework and lags de-escalation.

Inspector presence both constrains covert expansion and enables verified downblending. The June 2026 MOU conditions HEU disposition on IAEA-supervised on-site downblending, so access is the gating variable for stockpile reduction.

Growth in Iranian HEU is the explicit trigger cited by Saudi, Turkish and Egyptian officials for their own hedging, and by MBS in his repeated statement that Riyadh will match an Iranian weapon. Policy responses lag the technical fact by about a year.

Stockpile growth is Israel's declared red line and was the stated justification for both the June 2025 and February 2026 campaigns; detected reconstitution of enrichment is the most likely proximate trigger for the next round.
Regional hedging shortens Israeli and US preventive-action timelines and lowers the threshold for counter-proliferation strikes, a slow-acting positive feedback.

Rising Saudi threat perception raises the value of the US security and civil-nuclear package that Washington has explicitly conditioned on normalisation, pulling weakly in favour of a deal on a multi-year horizon.
War imposes fiscal and infrastructure damage and export interdiction that feed inflation and unrest, but with a substantial lag because the immediate effect is a rally-round-the-flag consolidation.

Export revenue funds the subsidy and security apparatus and anchors the rial. The collapse from 1.39 mb/d in January 2026 to a fraction of that is the proximate driver of 42%+ inflation and the December 2025 protest wave.

A domestically cornered leadership has a stronger incentive to externalise, and a weakened one has less to lose from chokepoint interdiction. Iran's Hormuz and Gulf-state attacks intensified as its internal position deteriorated.

Counter-intuitive but historically observed: sustained triple-digit oil raises the domestic political cost of the conflict for the US administration and for European and Asian sponsors, generating diplomatic pressure toward settlement. The June 2026 MOU followed the March-April price spike.
Lebanon is a component of the composite and the largest single source of casualties in the 2026 regional war (4,328 killed), so it contributes both directly and through escalation spillover.

Riyadh has conditioned normalisation on an irreversible path to Palestinian statehood, which in practice means visible progress through phases 2 and 3 of the 20-point plan: ISF deployment, Palestinian Authority reform and a political horizon.

key_uncertainties: Whether the late-July 2026 US strike pause becomes a durable ceasefire or merely the interval before a fourth round. The 60-day clock from the 17 June MOU expires in mid-August 2026, and Iran states no negotiations are currently under way.

The physical location and condition of Iran's roughly 441 kg of 60% HEU and of the thousands of centrifuges Israeli intelligence believes were relocated to Pickaxe Mountain. This is the single largest information gap in the domain and it drives every proliferation branch. Iran's claim that the material is irretrievably 'under the rubble' is unverified and self-serving in both directions.
Whether Iran has taken a weaponisation decision. The March 2026 US worldwide threat assessment says no, but the IAEA has had no access for over a year and the assessment rests on thin collection.

Who actually exercises authority in Tehran. Mojtaba Khamenei has not appeared in public since 8 March 2026 and communicates only in writing; it is unclear whether he governs, whether the IRGC does, or whether he is even in the country.
Whether the 27 October Israeli election produces a government able to trade two-state language for Saudi normalisation, and whether Netanyahu survives it.

Whether Gulf states remain non-belligerent after repeated Iranian missile and drone strikes on their territory, and whether the nuclear dimension of the Saudi-Pakistan Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement is ever tested. Pakistani officials have made directly contradictory public statements about it.

Whether Houthi interdiction of Bab el-Mandeb persists independently of US-Iran de-escalation. The Houthis have their own escalation logic and their July 2026 blockade targets Saudi rather than Israeli shipping.

The fundamentals-implied oil price under a fully reopened Hormuz. Most OPEC+ spare capacity is physically inside the Gulf and therefore Hormuz-dependent, so the conventional spare-capacity cushion may be largely illusory in exactly the scenarios where it is needed.
Whether the United States actually resumes nuclear explosive testing, and how that interacts with Gulf and East Asian hedging following the February 2026 expiry of New START.
Egypt's capacity to absorb another year of depressed Suez revenue on top of roughly $10bn of capital outflow since February 2026, and whether Saudi crude rerouting through Suez partially offsets it.
Whether Syria's al-Sharaa government can conclude a security agreement with Israel and complete SDF integration, or whether Syria reverts to a contested space that Iran can re-enter.
surprises_2026: 28 Feb 2026, 01:15: the US and Israel launched Operation Epic Fury / Operation Roaring Lion against Iran. Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was assassinated in the opening hours. Stated objectives were destruction of Iran's ballistic missile arsenal and production, its navy, and its defence industrial base, not formally regime change.

8 Mar 2026: the Assembly of Experts appointed Mojtaba Khamenei as the third Supreme Leader. As of late July 2026 he has never appeared in public, communicating only in writing, and his whereabouts are the subject of open speculation.

2-4 Mar 2026: the IRGC declared the Strait of Hormuz closed to US and Israel-allied shipping. This produced the first sustained >=50% Hormuz disruption in history. Gulf producers (Iraq, Saudi, Kuwait, UAE, Qatar, Bahrain) shut in 7.5 mb/d in March and 9.1 mb/d in April; the IEA called it the largest supply disruption in the history of the oil market.
9 Mar 2026: Brent hit $116.29, the highest since 2022, with physical cargoes reportedly trading $130-150. Brent rose roughly 51-65% during March, the largest monthly gain on record.
2 Mar 2026: a full 2026 Lebanon war began. Lebanon's Ministry of Public Health reports 4,328 killed and 12,229 wounded, the largest single casualty category of the regional war.
8 Apr 2026: a Pakistan-brokered US-Iran ceasefire took effect after more than five weeks of fighting, allowing partial Hormuz reopening. Iran re-restricted passage on 19 Apr.

16 Apr, 23 Apr, 15 May and 1 Jun 2026: a chain of short Israel-Lebanon and Israel-Hezbollah ceasefire extensions. Hezbollah initially rejected the 3 June Israel-Lebanon deal; Qassem stated Hezbollah will not return to the pre-March status quo.

17 Jun 2026: Trump and Pezeshkian signed remotely a 14-point US-Iran memorandum of understanding (the Islamabad Memorandum) providing a 60-day ceasefire extension, an Iranian pledge not to acquire nuclear weapons, and IAEA-supervised on-site downblending of the HEU stockpile. On 23 Jun the US issued sweeping oil sanctions waivers.

6-9 Jul 2026: Iran attacked at least nine commercial vessels in and near Hormuz over a dispute about which transit lanes vessels must use, including the Qatari LNG carrier Al-Rekayyat. The US revoked Iran's oil sales authorisation on 7 Jul and Trump declared the deal 'over' at the NATO summit.
12-13 Jul 2026: Iran fired missiles and drones at five Gulf states plus Jordan, including ballistic missiles at Al Udeid in Qatar and drone strikes on US assets in Kuwait, Bahrain, the UAE and Oman.

18 Jul 2026: Iranian ballistic missiles struck Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, killing two US service members with one missing; there were four separate Iranian missile attacks on US forces in Jordan in a single week. Total US war dead stand at 13-15.
July 2026: thirteen consecutive nights of US bombing of Iran, alongside a US naval interdiction campaign disabling roughly one Iranian-linked ship per day.

20-23 Jul 2026: Hormuz weekly transits fell to 53 vessels, down 66% week on week, with tanker and gas-carrier crossings falling from 90 to 30. Houthis resumed Red Sea attacks (MT Encelia, MT Layla) and declared a total blockade of Saudi-linked shipping, driving Bab el-Mandeb oil exports to near zero and forcing Saudi Arabia to reroute Asian crude via Suez (about 30 extra days of transit).
23 Jul 2026: Brent topped $100 for the first time since May; by 28 July it had fallen roughly 16% in three sessions to $87.53 as the US paused strikes and Iran said it was not negotiating.

July 2026: Saudi Arabia and the US signed a 30-year civil nuclear cooperation agreement. On 23 July Trump said it bars uranium enrichment and is conditioned on Saudi accession to the Abraham Accords. In May 2026 Riyadh had publicly rejected normalisation absent an irreversible path to Palestinian statehood.

26 Jul 2026: Israel's cabinet approved entry of the International Stabilization Force into Gaza, with an initial deployment of up to 200 troops from Kosovo, Albania and Morocco and possibly Kazakhstan. The Board of Peace announced a civilian 'pilot zone' at Tel Sultan near Rafah.

17 Jul 2026: the Knesset dissolved. Israeli elections are set for 27 October 2026, the last possible date, making this the first Israeli coalition in four decades to serve a full term. A Kan 11 poll gives the opposition bloc 69 seats to the coalition's 51, with Eisenkot's Yashar level with Likud.

26 Jul 2026: Syria's President al-Sharaa said Damascus is negotiating a multilateral security agreement with Israel that could lead to a comprehensive peace, while preserving Syria's claim to the Golan. A Syrian government-SDF integration agreement was signed on 29 January 2026 but implementation is delayed.

Iran's economy: the rial passed 1.47 million to the dollar in early January 2026, CPI inflation exceeds 42% with food inflation around 75%, and protests spread to all 31 provinces from 28 December 2025 before being suppressed by mass arrests, executions and prolonged internet blackouts.

February 2026: New START expired. The US publicly accused China of conducting secret supercritical nuclear tests and signalled intent to resume US nuclear testing for the first time since 1992, though the Energy Secretary said initial tests would be non-critical.

War-risk insurance for Hormuz transits rose from about 0.25% of hull value pre-war to 3-10% (market norm around 5%), equivalent to $3-10m per voyage for a $100m tanker, with some underwriters withdrawing cover entirely.

The June 2026 IAEA reports show continued total loss of monitoring: no access to any of Iran's four declared enrichment facilities, unknown status of the newly declared Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant, and no verification of the size, composition or location of the enriched uranium stockpile. Iran's foreign minister said on 15 March 2026 that the material is 'under the rubble' with no plan to recover it.

Cumulative regional war deaths reached roughly 9,000-18,000 by late July 2026 across trackers: Iran 3,468 officially (up to 6,000+ per US and Israeli estimates), Lebanon 4,328, Israel 57, US 13-15, Iraq 119+, UAE 13, Kuwait 10.
